results.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
results.proof_sketch: The sparse-to-target ratio is m^(4/3)/(n√m)=m^(5/6)/n, so it is at most one exactly when m≤n^(6/5). The dense-to-target ratio is n/√m, which is polylogarithmic when m≥n²/log^C n. Writing m=n^a, the two available bounds cross when 4a/3=2, namely a=3/2. Before this point the ratio exponent 5a/6−1 increases; afterward 1−a/2 decreases. Both equal 1/4 at the crossing.

results.claim: Reachability-rectangle identity: if R is reflexive reachability immediately before inserting u→v, A={x:xRu}, D={y:vRy}, and R⁺ is reachability afterward, then R⁺=R∪(A×D). Hence an insertion sequence evolves reachability exactly by monotone union with these time-dependent ancestor–descendant rectangles.
results.proof_sketch: Every new x-to-y path must use u→v. Choose a simple such path, which uses that edge once; its prefix is an old x-to-u path and its suffix is an old v-to-y path, so (x,y)∈A×D. Conversely, for x∈A and y∈D, concatenating x→…→u, the inserted edge, and v→…→y proves xR⁺y. Old paths persist, proving both inclusions. Iterating the identity gives the sequence statement. In the acyclic order-violating branch, the balanced B×F rectangle lies inside A×D and wholly outside R because each f∈F precedes each b∈B in the old topological order.

results.claim: Corrected balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, either v already reaches u, so the insertion closes a cycle, or one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological after the insertion, and all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
results.proof_sketch: Use reflexive reachability and let D be the descendants of v and A the ancestors of u. If v reaches u, report the cycle and make no cut assertion. Otherwise D and A are disjoint: a common vertex would give a v-to-u path. Sweep cuts from immediately before v through immediately before u. The value h=|D on the left|−|A on the right| starts negative and is nonnegative at the last cut: A has only u there, while D contains at least v. Crossing one vertex raises h by zero or one because D∩A=∅, so some cut has h=0; it occurs after v enters the left side, making the common size positive. In the stable reorder, a reversed old edge inside L would have type F→L\F, contradicting descendant closure; inside R it would have type R\B→B, contradicting ancestor closure; and an edge F→B would give a v-to-u path. The new edge is directed from u∈B to v∈F. Finally every b∈B reaches every f∈F through b→…→u→v→…→f, whereas f preceded b before insertion, so no b reached f in the old topological order.

results.claim: Structural reduction for the balanced-cut route: suppose a combinatorial ordered-reachability boundary oracle can absorb all edge insertions and stable block reorders in total Õ(n+m+Σ_i q_i) time, and on each violating insertion either reports an old v-to-u path or returns a cut c with F=D(v)∩L_c, B=A(u)∩R_c, and |B|=|F|=q_i>0. Then it yields an incremental topological-sort algorithm with total update time Õ(n√m).
results.proof_sketch: Keep the order in a balanced sequence tree. A forward insertion needs no reorder. On a violating insertion, the path answer certifies a cycle. Otherwise apply the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B); the balanced-cut lemma proves that it is topological. Every pair in B_i×F_i is outside old reachability by the old order and enters it through the new edge. Thus different updates charge disjoint first-time pairs, so Σ_i q_i²≤n(n−1). For k≤m such updates, Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σ_i q_i≤√(kΣ_i q_i²)=O(n√m). Sequence-tree work is Õ(Σ_i q_i), and the oracle has the same bound plus Õ(n+m). After duplicates are discarded, m≤n², hence m≤n√m; a terminal O(n)-size cycle certificate also fits. This proves the transfer. The adjacency-list heap implementation in the next claim realizes this oracle only with the additional scan term A, so constructing the stipulated oracle remains the intermediate open task.

results.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
results.proof_sketch: Apply the corrected cycle-or-cut lemma. For non-cycle violating update i, write |B_i|=|F_i|=q_i. Its q_i² product pairs become reachable for the first time. Reachability is monotone, so these products are disjoint between updates and Σq_i²≤n(n−1). If there are k≤m such updates, Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σq_i≤√(kΣq_i²)=O(n√m). Min/max heaps enumerate the two searches in topological order; non-root heap insertions are charged to scanned entries in A. A balanced sequence tree performs stable extraction and reinsertion in Õ(q_i), while edge storage and search initialization cost Õ(m). The first cycle-forming update costs at most Õ(n+A) and terminates processing. Hence the total is Õ(m+n√m+A). Under the stated directional-degree condition, A=Õ(Σq_i+n). For distinct simple edges m≤n², so m is also O(n√m).

results.claim: The rectangle reformulation cannot be implemented by eagerly materializing every newly reachable pair within the target bound: there is an insertion sequence with n=2r and m=2r−1 whose final insertion creates exactly r² new reachability pairs. Thus any implementation doing Ω(1) work per newly created pair takes Ω(n²), not Õ(n√m), on this sequence.
results.proof_sketch: Take disjoint chains x₁→⋯→x_r and y₁→⋯→y_r, inserted in the displayed topological order, and finally insert x_r→y₁. Before the last insertion no x reaches any y. Its ancestor set at x_r is all r x-vertices and its descendant set at y₁ is all r y-vertices. The rectangle identity therefore adds exactly {x₁,…,x_r}×{y₁,…,y_r}, of size r². The whole sequence uses 2(r−1)+1=2r−1 edges on 2r vertices. Consequently eager per-pair work is Θ(r²)=Θ(n²), whereas n√m=Θ(r^(3/2)); their ratio is Θ(√n), larger than every polylogarithm. This only rules out eager cell-by-cell closure and leaves compressed or lazy representations possible.

results.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
results.proof_sketch: Use initial order v,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r and first insert v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z for all i,j. Then insert u_i→v in increasing i. Immediately before update i, the order is u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,u_i,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r, so the cut between v and u_i has F={v}, B={u_i}, and q=1. Vertex u_i already reaches z and every w_j, and it has no proper ancestor; therefore the only new proper reachability pair is (u_i,v). Nevertheless v retains its r outgoing entries, all of which an ordinary expansion rescans on each of the r updates. There are 3r initial edges and r violating insertions, while the scans total r².

results.claim: Semantically, the balanced search may be restricted to the old topological interval [v,u]: ignoring forward neighbors after u and backward neighbors before v preserves cycle detection and produces the same descendant/ancestor intersections needed by every cut between v and u.
results.proof_sketch: Every old edge is forward in the maintained order. Hence every vertex on a v-to-u path lies between v and u, so restricting both searches to that interval cannot hide a cycle certificate. For a cut c between v and u, a path from v to a vertex at or left of c cannot first leave [v,u] and return, because positions strictly increase along every nontrivial path; therefore the restricted forward search recovers D∩L exactly. Reversing the argument, the restricted backward search recovers A∩R exactly. The sweep, stable reorder, and fresh-pair proof consume only these two intersections. This establishes semantic correctness, but assumes no efficient dynamic range-reporting implementation.

results.claim: Even perfect filtering of adjacency entries outside the active interval does not make full-list balanced expansion Õ(n√m): for every p,q≥2 there is a block-swap sequence on n=pq vertices and m=[pq(q−1)+p(p−1)]/2 edges with p(p−1)/2 violating updates, each having |B|=|F|=q, whose selected-block internal entries alone are rescanned p(p−1)q(q−1)/2 times. Setting p=q² gives m=Θ(n^(4/3)) and Θ(n²) scans, a Θ(n^(1/3)) factor above n√m.
results.proof_sketch: Form p consecutive blocks C₀,…,C_(p−1), each a complete q-vertex DAG in its internal order. For j=1,…,p−1 and a=0,…,j−1, the current order has C_a immediately before C_j; insert an edge from the sink of C_j to the source of C_a and apply the stable reorder, which swaps those blocks. Inductively the processed prefix is reversed. There is no old C_a-to-C_j path, so every insertion is acyclic. At the intervening cut, the descendants of C_a's source on the left are exactly C_a and the ancestors of C_j's sink on the right are exactly C_j; thus q_i=q and the q² fresh pairs are precisely C_j×C_a. Full expansion scans q(q−1)/2 internal forward entries of C_a and the same number of internal backward entries of C_j, none removable by outside-interval filtering. Summing over the p(p−1)/2 block pairs gives the stated count. For p=q², n=q³, m=q⁴−(q³+q²)/2, and the scan lower bound is Θ(q⁶), whereas n√m=Θ(q⁵).

final_writeup:
This remains partial progress: it does not give the requested unconditional Õ(n√m) combinatorial algorithm for arbitrary-degree insertion sequences.

The two bounds stated in the source give Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). They meet the target for m≤n^(6/5) and, up to logarithms, for m near n²; their worst intermediate-density gap is Õ(n^(1/4)).

A structural reformulation makes the remaining task precise. Let R be reflexive reachability before inserting u→v, let A be the old ancestors of u, and let D be the old descendants of v. Reachability afterward is exactly

R⁺ = R ∪ (A×D).

Indeed, a new path splits at its use of u→v into an old path to u and an old path from v; the converse follows by concatenation. Thus incremental reachability evolves by monotone union with ancestor–descendant rectangles. The balanced-cut construction does not need to materialize a whole rectangle: on an acyclic order violation it needs only equally sized boundary slices B⊆A and F⊆D separated in reverse old-order position.

This yields a precise sufficient intermediate problem for the balanced-cut route. Suppose a combinatorial ordered-reachability boundary oracle absorbs insertions and order changes in total Õ(n+m+Σq_i) time and, for every violation, either returns an old v-to-u path or an exact cut with F=D∩L_c, B=A∩R_c, and |B|=|F|=q_i. Maintain the order in a balanced sequence tree and replace it by (L_c minus F), B, F, (R_c minus B). Descendant closure, ancestor closure, and absence of an old v-to-u path prove this order topological. Every B_i×F_i pair becomes reachable for the first time, so Σq_i²≤n(n−1), whence Σq_i=O(n√m) by Cauchy–Schwarz. The oracle would therefore transfer directly to the target bound.

The explicit heap-and-adjacency implementation from the parent realizes this reduction with total cost Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of outgoing entries scanned from selected forward vertices plus incoming entries scanned from selected backward vertices. It proves the target when A=Õ(n√m), including the stated polylogarithmic relevant-direction-degree class, but not in general.

The rectangle view also rules out one apparent repair. Build two disjoint r-vertex chains and then insert an edge from the first chain's sink to the second chain's source. The complete sequence has n=2r and m=2r−1, but the last edge creates all r² cross-chain reachability pairs. Consequently an eager representation spending constant work per new pair costs Θ(n²), polynomially above Õ(n√m). A successful oracle must keep such rectangles compressed or lazy.

Restricting searches to the old interval [v,u] is semantically valid because positions strictly increase along old DAG paths. This removes irrelevant outside-interval entries, but does not solve the problem. In the verified block-swap family, p complete q-vertex DAG blocks undergo p(p−1)/2 adjacent swaps. Each update has |B|=|F|=q and creates its q² block rectangle for the first time, yet full expansion rescans q(q−1) internal block entries. With p=q², n=q³ and m=Θ(q⁴)=Θ(n^(4/3)), while these scans total Θ(q⁶)=Θ(n²), versus target Θ(q⁵).

Thus the structural reformulation isolates the unresolved requirement: support ordered boundary extraction from a monotone union of highly overlapping reachability rectangles without eagerly expanding either the rectangles or repeatedly selected dense adjacency regions. Neither the reduction nor the two obstructions supply that data structure, so the arbitrary-degree intermediate-density case and the exact open target remain unresolved.
